group.passage: Checking tomorrow's weather takes most of us only a few seconds. It is easy to forget that the very idea of predicting the weather was once mocked, and that the man who first offered forecasts to the public paid a heavy price for his ambition. That man was Robert FitzRoy, a naval officer who had once commanded the famous ship HMS Beagle. In 1854, he was put in charge of a small new government office whose task was to study the weather at sea. Five years later, a fierce storm struck the coasts of Britain and wrecked more than a hundred ships. Among them was the Royal Charter, which was on the final stage of a two-month voyage from Australia when it was driven onto rocks in Wales. About 460 people on board died. FitzRoy was convinced that the disaster could have been predicted. He arranged for stations along the coast to send measurements of air pressure, wind and temperature to London by telegraph every morning. By comparing these reports, his office could detect a storm before it arrived. In February 1861, it issued its first storm warning, and cones and drums were raised on poles in harbors to alert sailors. That August, FitzRoy went a step further: he printed a forecast for the general public in The Times, the first of its kind. Not everyone welcomed the move. His forecasts were often wrong, and many scientists remained skeptical that the weather could ever be predicted. Although he persisted in refining his methods, the criticism wore him down. After his death in 1865, a government report recommended that forecasting be stopped, and both the forecasts and the storm warnings came to an end. Public demand brought the warnings back in 1867, and forecasts for the public finally returned in 1879. FitzRoy's service for sailors survives today as the Shipping Forecast, which is believed to be the oldest national forecasting service still in operation anywhere. Supercomputers have long since replaced telegraphs, yet the goal remains the same. In 2022, the United Nations set the goal of covering every person on Earth with early warning systems before 2027 is over, since only half of all countries report having adequate ones.

translation_zh.text:
天氣預報的誕生

查看明天的天氣，我們大多數人只要花幾秒鐘。我們很容易忘記，預測天氣這個想法本身曾經被人嘲笑，而第一個向大眾提供天氣預報的人，也為他的抱負付出了沉重的代價。

這個人是羅伯特‧費茲羅伊，一位曾經指揮著名的「小獵犬號」的海軍軍官。1854 年，他被任命主持一個新成立的小型政府辦公室，任務是研究海上的天氣。五年後，一場猛烈的暴風侵襲英國沿岸，毀了一百多艘船。其中包括「皇家憲章號」，它正處於從澳洲出發、為期兩個月航程的最後一段，卻被吹上威爾斯的岩岸。船上約 460 人喪生。

費茲羅伊深信這場災難原本可以被預測。他安排沿岸各測站每天早上用電報把氣壓、風和溫度的測量值傳到倫敦。藉由比對這些報告，他的辦公室能在暴風來臨前就察覺到它。1861 年 2 月，辦公室發出第一次暴風警報，港口的桿子上升起圓錐形和鼓形的信號來警告水手。同年 8 月，費茲羅伊更進一步：他在《泰晤士報》刊出一則給一般大眾看的天氣預報，這是史上第一次。

並不是每個人都歡迎這個舉動。他的預報常常不準，許多科學家也一直懷疑天氣究竟能不能被預測。雖然他堅持不斷改進方法，批評還是讓他身心俱疲。他在 1865 年去世後，一份政府報告建議停止預報，於是預報和暴風警報都告終止。在民眾的要求下，警報於 1867 年恢復，而給大眾的預報則一直到 1879 年才終於重新出現。

費茲羅伊為水手設立的服務，今天仍以「航海天氣預報」的形式存在，被認為是世界上仍在運作的全國性預報服務中歷史最悠久的一個。超級電腦早已取代了電報，但目標依然相同。2022 年，聯合國訂下目標，要在 2027 年結束前讓地球上每一個人都有預警系統保護，因為只有一半的國家表示擁有足夠完善的預警系統。
